paragraphs: This paper develops a two-step way to compute the Wasserstein distance used in Wasserstein generative adversarial networks. The method separates the objective into a convex component, solved with linear programming, and a nonconvex remainder, approximated by a deep neural network. This division gives different computational treatments to parts of the problem with different mathematical properties.

The authors prove that their formulation is equivalent to the discrete Monge–Kantorovich dual formulation. They also bound the error from approximation and from extending the distance calculation from discrete to continuous distributions. Thus, optimizing an exact distance formulation does not mean every neural-network approximation is error-free. The approach removes the need for the weight clipping previously used in WGANs.

On synthetic data, the method computes the distance more accurately. Experiments on MNIST, LSUN, and CIFAR-10 report greater efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art WGAN methods while maintaining comparable image quality. These findings connect a mathematically grounded objective with practical gains in distance estimation and image generation.
icml-2018-a-two-step-computation-of-the-.tldr: A two-step Wasserstein-distance formulation combines linear programming and neural approximation, improving reported efficiency while preserving comparable generated-image quality.

paragraphs: This paper treats deep learning as a discrete-time optimal control problem. That perspective provides necessary conditions for an optimal solution and supports training procedures that do not require gradients with respect to the trainable parameters. It is especially relevant when weights must belong to a discrete set, where ordinary continuous parameter updates do not directly respect the permitted values.

The authors introduce a discrete-time method of successive approximations based on Pontryagin’s maximum principle. They derive a rigorous error estimate that helps explain the method’s behavior and how it can be stabilized. The theoretical contribution therefore concerns both the formulation of training and the dynamics of the resulting algorithm.

The methods are applied to neural networks with discrete-valued weights and achieve competitive performance. For ternary networks, the learned weights are also very sparse. The authors suggest that this combination could be useful for deployment on devices with limited memory. That deployment benefit is presented as a possibility, while competitive performance and sparse ternary weights are reported findings.
icml-2018-an-optimal-control-approach-to.tldr: An optimal-control formulation enables training without parameter gradients and produces competitive discrete-weight networks, including very sparse ternary networks.

paragraphs: Distributed training can lose efficiency when workers run at different speeds or share congested networks. Synchronous methods must coordinate progress, while centralized asynchronous methods can overload a parameter server. This paper proposes asynchronous decentralized stochastic gradient descent, AD-PSGD, to combine tolerance for heterogeneous workers with efficient communication.

The theoretical analysis establishes the optimal O(1/√K) convergence rate associated with SGD and linear speedup with the number of workers. These results support the algorithm’s scalability within the analyzed setting. Empirically, it outperforms the compared decentralized, centralized asynchronous, and standard data-parallel methods, often by orders of magnitude in heterogeneous environments.

For ResNet-50 training on ImageNet with up to 128 GPUs, AD-PSGD has similar convergence measured in epochs to AllReduce-SGD. In the tested network-sharing high-performance computing environment, epochs can be up to four to eight times faster than with synchronous alternatives. The distinction matters: the reported advantage combines similar learning progress per epoch with substantially less elapsed time for that progress.
icml-2018-asynchronous-decentralized-par.tldr: AD-PSGD combines asynchronous decentralized training with convergence guarantees and substantial reported speedups in heterogeneous computing environments.

paragraphs: Learning several tasks through shared features can let them benefit from one another, but it can also spread unreliable information. This harmful interaction is called negative transfer. Deep Asymmetric Multitask Feature Learning addresses it by giving tasks different levels of influence over the shared representation instead of treating their contributions symmetrically.

The method introduces an asymmetric autoencoder term. Reliable predictors for easier tasks contribute strongly to feature learning, while unreliable predictors for harder tasks have their influence suppressed. The intended result is a less noisy shared representation. Harder tasks can still benefit from knowledge contributed by reliable predictors through those common latent features.

Sharing knowledge through features is also presented as more scalable and efficient than asymmetric transfer directly between tasks. Across multiple multitask-learning and image-classification benchmarks, the proposed model significantly outperforms the compared symmetric and asymmetric alternatives. The reported results support the value of controlling who shapes shared features, as well as allowing multiple tasks to use them.
icml-2018-deep-asymmetric-multi-task-fea.tldr: Deep-AMTFL reduces negative transfer by letting reliable task predictors exert more influence on shared features than unreliable ones.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when actions come from a continuous range and small changes can produce very different outcomes. Simulated curling provides the case study. The central challenge is choosing precise actions in a setting where methods designed around discrete choices are not suitable for capturing the sensitivity described by the authors.

The proposed framework combines self-play reinforcement learning with a continuous search algorithm that uses kernel regression. This gives the system a way to search directly within the continuous action space. Training starts with supervised learning and then proceeds through self-play using a high-fidelity curling simulator, without relying on hand-crafted features.

The resulting program outperforms existing curling programs that use several hand-crafted features and wins an international digital curling competition. These findings demonstrate success for the combined learning and search framework in simulated curling. The contribution is particularly relevant to action selection where precision matters: the system learns its representations while retaining a search procedure suited to continuously varying decisions.
icml-2018-deep-reinforcement-learning-in.tldr: A self-play framework combining neural learning with continuous action search achieves strong simulated-curling performance without hand-crafted features.

paragraphs: This paper asks how fairness rules affect the people subject to decisions after those decisions have been made. A criterion evaluated at a single moment may look favorable while producing different consequences over time. The authors therefore examine improvement, stagnation, and decline in a variable representing group well-being.

Even in a model with just one step of feedback, common fairness criteria do not generally ensure improvement. In some cases, they can cause harm where an unconstrained objective would not. The paper fully characterizes the delayed effects of three standard criteria within its model and identifies regimes in which their behavior differs qualitatively.

The analysis also finds that a natural form of measurement error expands the regime where fairness criteria perform favorably. Together, these results make both measurement and temporal feedback central to evaluating fairness. They do not establish that fairness constraints always help or always harm; they show why the consequences depend on the modeled setting and how outcomes are measured.
icml-2018-delayed-impact-of-fair-machine.tldr: A feedback model shows that static fairness criteria can have harmful delayed effects in some regimes, making measurement and temporal consequences essential to evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper addresses label shift: class frequencies change between training and deployment, while the distribution of observations within each class stays fixed. The goal is to detect and measure that change, then adjust a classifier without needing labels for the test data. This separates a specific kind of distribution shift from changes in how classes themselves appear.

Black Box Shift Estimation uses a predictor’s outputs to reduce the dimensionality of the estimation problem. The predictor can be biased, inaccurate, or uncalibrated, provided its confusion matrix is invertible. Better predictors yield tighter estimates, but perfect prediction is not required for the approach to work.

The authors prove consistency, give error bounds, and develop a statistical test for detecting shift. They also use the estimated class frequencies to correct classifiers. Experiments report accurate estimates and improved predictions, including on high-dimensional natural images. These results support using an existing predictor as a tool for adaptation under the stated label-shift and invertibility conditions.
icml-2018-detecting-and-correcting-for-l.tldr: BBSE detects and estimates label shift without test labels using black-box predictors whose confusion matrices are invertible.

paragraphs: This paper estimates a low-rank Markov chain from observed trajectories. The object being learned is its transition matrix, which describes how the process moves between states. By imposing a rank constraint, the estimator incorporates a compressed structure into the estimation problem rather than treating all transition behavior as unrestricted.

The proposed estimator maximizes likelihood subject to that rank constraint, producing a nonconvex optimization problem. The authors establish statistical upper bounds for the discrepancy between the estimated and true transition matrices, using both Kullback–Leibler divergence and an ℓ2 risk measure. The estimator also reveals a compressed state space, connecting statistical estimation with a simpler representation of the chain.

To compute the estimator, the paper develops a difference-of-convex-functions programming algorithm for the nonsmooth, rank-constrained objective and establishes convergence results. Experiments show better empirical performance than the compared popular approaches. The contribution therefore combines an estimator, guarantees about its statistical error, and an optimization method for tackling the structured estimation problem.
icml-2018-estimation-of-markov-chain-via.tldr: Rank-constrained likelihood estimation learns low-rank Markov chains with statistical error bounds and an algorithm for the resulting nonconvex problem.

paragraphs: Value Iteration Networks provide differentiable planning components that can be trained as part of a larger navigation system. However, they can be difficult to optimize and sensitive to random seeds. This paper revisits their architecture to understand those problems through the lens of recurrent neural networks.

The authors describe VINs as recurrent convolutional networks using an unconventional max-pooling activation. This perspective motivates replacing the update mechanism with standard gated recurrent equations, producing the Gated Path Planning Network. The underlying argument is that gating could alleviate optimization difficulties while retaining a learned planning component within an end-to-end differentiable system.

Experiments show improvements over VINs in learning speed, sensitivity to hyperparameters, iteration count, and generalization. The performance gap persists across different maze sizes and transition types. The method also succeeds in a challenging three-dimensional environment where the planner receives only first-person RGB images. These are empirical findings supporting the architectural change across the evaluated navigation settings, rather than a universal guarantee about all planning tasks.
icml-2018-gated-path-planning-networks-b.tldr: Gated Path Planning Networks use recurrent gating to improve empirical training behavior and navigation performance over Value Iteration Networks.

paragraphs: To scale Gaussian process regression, aggregation methods train multiple experts separately and then combine their predictions. This division supports distributed computation, but the final combination still needs to be statistically reliable and computationally efficient. The paper identifies a tension in existing approaches: predictions can be inconsistent, or aggregation can take substantial time.

The authors first prove inconsistency for typical aggregation methods using disjoint or random partitions of the data. They then propose an aggregation model designed to provide consistent predictions efficiently. It retains closed-form inference and aggregation, as well as the ability to parallelize training and use distributed computing.

The theoretical and empirical analyses support improved performance from the new approach. Its consistency means that predictions converge to the true underlying function as training size approaches infinity in the analyzed setting. That is an asymptotic property, rather than a claim of exact prediction from a finite dataset. The contribution connects scalable expert-based computation with a statistically meaningful target for what additional data should achieve.
icml-2018-generalized-robust-bayesian-co.tldr: A Gaussian-process aggregation method combines efficient distributed computation with predictions that consistently approach the underlying function.

paragraphs: This paper studies constrained convex optimization when both the objective and constraints are finite sums of loss functions. Such problems arise in machine learning, including Neyman–Pearson classification. The authors examine an existing inexact Newton level-set method and introduce a new feasible level-set method for this class of problems.

Both approaches move a level parameter toward optimality using information supplied by an oracle. That oracle must provide upper and lower bounds on a level function, along with an affine function that bounds it from below. Constructing this information is a central part of making the overall methods computationally usable.

The authors express the level function through a saddle-point problem using conjugate and perspective transformations of the losses. They then build the oracle with a stochastic variance-reduced gradient method and a specially chosen Bregman divergence. This choice makes each proximal update available in closed form. The paper analyzes the total complexity of both level-set methods, linking their outer progress to the work needed for the oracle.
icml-2018-level-set-methods-for-finite-s.tldr: A saddle-point oracle with closed-form proximal updates supports two level-set methods for finite-sum constrained convex optimization.

paragraphs: Image restoration aims to recover a clean signal from corrupted observations. Noise2Noise asks whether learning this mapping actually requires clean examples during training. Using statistical reasoning, the paper shows that it is possible to train restoration models using only corrupted data, with performance matching and sometimes exceeding training that uses clean data.

The approach does not require explicit image priors or likelihood models describing the corruption. This matters because the training setup can learn useful restoration behavior from noisy observations without supplying those additional models. The claim is that corrupted examples can be sufficient for successful learning, rather than that every possible corruption process must permit the same result.

The practical demonstrations cover photographic noise removal, denoising synthetic Monte Carlo images, and reconstruction of undersampled MRI scans. These involve different sources of corruption, yet the reported model learns restoration from noisy data alone. Together, the examples support the paper’s central finding across several restoration settings: clean training data need not always be the ingredient that makes accurate reconstruction possible.
icml-2018-noise2noise-learning-image-res.tldr: Noise2Noise shows that image restoration can be learned from corrupted data alone, sometimes matching or exceeding training with clean data.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why generative adversarial network training can behave unpredictably. The authors study a simple parametric model that nevertheless exhibits several familiar failures: vanishing gradients, mode collapse, divergence, and oscillation. Its role is to make problematic training behavior accessible to rigorous analysis within a manageable mathematical setting.

Despite the model’s nonconvexity, the authors prove a sharp difference between two ways of handling the discriminator. With an optimal discriminator, the GAN converges. When discriminator updates instead use first-order approximations, the analyzed dynamics become unstable and exhibit mode collapse. The contrast ties the behavior to how the discriminator’s contribution is computed.

The practical implication is deliberately qualified. Since first-order discriminator steps are common in GAN training, they might be one factor behind its difficulties. The theorem concerns the paper’s particular model; its relevance to broader practice is a suggested explanation. The work therefore provides a concrete mechanism for instability without asserting that first-order updates make every GAN fail.
icml-2018-on-the-limitations-of-first-or.tldr: In an analyzed GAN model, optimal discriminators yield convergence while first-order discriminator approximations produce instability and mode collapse.

paragraphs: Random feature maps extend random projections by applying nonlinear operations. Those nonlinearities make the maps useful, but also make their behavior harder to analyze. This paper studies the Gram matrix associated with such maps, focusing on its spectrum as a way to understand the structure created by the transformed data.

The analysis uses concentration phenomena from random matrix theory. Its setting is data drawn from Gaussian mixture models, with both the number of observations and their dimension large simultaneously. These specifications matter because the conclusions describe random feature behavior in that high-dimensional statistical setting, rather than arbitrary data without distributional structure.

The results clarify how the choice of nonlinearity interacts with the statistics of the data. That relationship is the practical motivation for the spectral analysis: understanding the transformed representation can inform better tuning of random-feature methods. The paper’s stated contribution is therefore an analytical account of what shapes these representations and how that understanding can guide methodological choices.
icml-2018-on-the-spectrum-of-random-feat.tldr: Random matrix analysis explains how nonlinear random features interact with high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture data through their Gram-matrix spectrum.

paragraphs: Open category detection asks whether a test example belongs to a class absent from the known training categories. This paper seeks guarantees for detecting these unfamiliar examples, which it calls aliens. It studies a particular training setup that makes the problem more structured than detection under general assumptions.

The algorithm receives two datasets: a clean set containing only target categories and an unlabeled contaminated set containing some alien examples. The alien fraction is denoted by alpha, and the method assumes a known upper bound on that fraction. Under this assumption, the authors develop PAC-style guarantees on the alien detection rate while aiming to keep false alarms low.

This separates the guaranteed detection objective from the additional goal of avoiding unnecessary alarms. Experiments on synthetic and standard benchmark datasets identify regimes where the algorithm can be effective and establish a baseline for further work. The contribution is a theoretically supported step for the stated two-dataset setting, rather than a guarantee for every open-category problem.
icml-2018-open-category-detection-with-p.tldr: Given clean and contaminated training sets plus a bound on contamination, an algorithm provides PAC-style guarantees for detecting unfamiliar categories.

paragraphs: This paper studies how distributing regression training affects prediction on unseen data. The setting is nonparametric regression in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and the algorithms use stochastic gradient methods with mini-batches and multiple passes through the data. The question is whether dividing the work can preserve strong statistical performance.

The authors show that distributed stochastic gradient methods retain optimal generalization error bounds when the partition level is not too large. This qualification is central: the result supports distribution up to an appropriate degree, rather than unlimited splitting. The theory also covers cases where the true regression function does not belong to the chosen hypothesis space.

Compared with earlier theory, the results broaden the settings covered and establish lower theoretical computational complexity than distributed kernel ridge regression and classic stochastic gradient methods. The significance is a joint statistical and computational result. Within the analyzed conditions, distributed training can reduce the theoretical work required while retaining an optimal bound on generalization error.
icml-2018-optimal-distributed-learning-w.tldr: Distributed multi-pass stochastic gradient methods retain optimal regression guarantees when data partitioning is sufficiently limited.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes least-squares regression methods that combine regularization with projection into a reduced space. The framework covers Hilbert spaces, including reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces used for nonparametric regression. The central issue is how much the problem can be compressed while preserving strong convergence guarantees.

The authors prove convergence results under a capacity assumption on the hypothesis space and a regularity condition on the target function. For randomized sketches, they obtain optimal rates when the sketch dimension scales with the effective dimension, up to a logarithmic factor. This provides a sufficient relationship between the size of the reduced problem and the statistical structure that must be retained.

Related results also follow for Nyström regularized methods. The rates depend on the data distribution and cover both attainable and non-attainable settings, allowing the target to lie inside or outside the hypothesis space. The contribution is a conditional theoretical justification for reduced-dimensional regression: appropriately sized projections can preserve optimal rates under the stated assumptions.
icml-2018-optimal-rates-of-sketched-regu.tldr: Under capacity and regularity assumptions, sufficiently large randomized sketches preserve optimal convergence rates for regularized least-squares regression.

paragraphs: Adjacency spectral embedding represents graph vertices as points in Euclidean space. This paper asks how to extend such a representation to a vertex that was not included in the original embedding. The goal parallels out-of-sample extensions in other dimensionality-reduction methods: use an existing learned representation to position a new observation.

The authors propose two approaches, one based on least squares and another on maximum likelihood. Under a random dot product graph model, both methods estimate the new vertex’s true latent position with the same error rate. This comparison gives a theoretical basis for two different estimation objectives within the specified graph model.

For the least-squares extension, the paper additionally proves a central limit theorem. As the graph becomes large, the estimate is asymptotically normal around the true latent position. This describes the form of estimation uncertainty beyond its rate alone. Together, the results establish both error-rate guarantees for the two extensions and a more detailed large-graph characterization for the least-squares approach.
icml-2018-out-of-sample-extension-of-gra.tldr: Two out-of-sample graph embedding methods achieve the same latent-position error rate under a random dot product graph model.

paragraphs: This paper revisits recurrent back-propagation, examining when it applies and how its requirements can be satisfied in deep neural networks. The authors show that the original approach can be unstable. They propose two alternatives: CG-RBP, based on conjugate gradients applied to normal equations, and Neumann-RBP, based on a Neumann series.

A key contribution is the relationship between Neumann-RBP and back-propagation through time, including its truncated version. Neumann-RBP has the same time complexity as truncated back-propagation through time but needs constant memory. By comparison, the truncated method’s memory use grows linearly with the number of truncation steps, making the distinction meaningful when more steps are considered.

The experiments cover associative memory with continuous Hopfield networks, document classification with graph neural networks on citation networks, and hyperparameter optimization for fully connected networks. Across these applications, the recurrent back-propagation variants are efficient and effective, especially Neumann-RBP. The stated scope is optimization of convergent recurrent neural networks, which is central to interpreting these results.
icml-2018-reviving-and-improving-recurre.tldr: Improved recurrent back-propagation variants train convergent recurrent networks effectively, with Neumann-RBP offering constant-memory computation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning algorithms contain nested computations whose structure can be irregular. Opportunities to distribute work appear at several levels, so building a scalable implementation involves more than parallelizing one isolated operation. This paper argues for software components that can be combined while keeping their distributed execution manageable.

The proposed organizing principle is top-down hierarchical control. Parallelism and resource requirements are packaged inside short-running compute tasks, allowing larger algorithms to coordinate components without exposing every internal execution detail. This composability is the central design idea: distributed pieces should remain reusable when assembled into different reinforcement learning algorithms.

RLlib implements this principle as scalable software primitives within the open-source Ray project. The paper demonstrates that these primitives support a broad range of algorithms with high performance, scalability, and substantial code reuse. Its contribution is therefore an architecture for implementing distributed reinforcement learning, connecting the structure of computation to the organization of reusable software rather than introducing a single new learning rule.
icml-2018-rllib-abstractions-for-distrib.tldr: RLlib uses composable distributed tasks and hierarchical control to support scalable reinforcement learning with substantial code reuse.

paragraphs: This paper introduces submodular hypergraphs for clustering problems where relationships among groups carry useful information. A hyperedge can involve several vertices, and different ways of cutting that hyperedge receive different submodular weights. This gives the model a way to represent how a partition separates a higher-order relationship.

The authors develop p-Laplacians for this family of hypergraphs and establish corresponding nodal domain theorems and k-way Cheeger inequalities. These results supply mathematical connections between spectral structure and partitioning. The purpose is to give the new hypergraph model theoretical machinery that can support clustering methods based on its spectra.

The paper also describes algorithms for computing the spectra of the 1-Laplacian and 2-Laplacian. Those computations form the basis of new spectral hypergraph clustering approaches. The contribution spans representation, theory, and algorithms: it specifies richer cut weights, develops the associated spectral objects, and provides ways to compute the objects used by the clustering methods.
icml-2018-submodular-hypergraphs-p-lapla.tldr: Submodular hypergraphs support cut-dependent higher-order relationships, with new spectral theory and algorithms for clustering.

paragraphs: This paper develops a random matrix framework for understanding how training evolves over time. It studies a single-layer linear network performing binary classification with gradient descent. The data setting has both a large number of observations and a large number of dimensions, bringing the analysis into a regime suited to random matrix methods.

The focus is learning dynamics rather than only the final trained model. The resulting analysis provides insights into overfitting, early stopping, and initialization. These questions concern different parts of the same process: where training begins, how it progresses, and when continued optimization may cease to be useful for generalization.

The scope of the established framework is the specified linear network and classification problem. The authors present it as a foundation for future analysis of more elaborate neural architectures and models. Its significance is that a tractable high-dimensional setting can reveal structure in training behavior and offer a starting point for studying questions that also arise in deeper networks.
icml-2018-the-dynamics-of-learning-a-ran.tldr: A random matrix framework analyzes gradient-descent dynamics in a high-dimensional linear classifier, informing questions about initialization, overfitting, and early stopping.

paragraphs: The Lasso fits a least-squares regression model with a penalty on the sum of absolute coefficient values. This paper studies the complexity of its entire regularization path as the penalty strength varies. Coefficients follow linear pieces along that path, and complexity is measured by the number of changes between those pieces.

There is a gap between observed and worst-case behavior. Exact path-following experiments exhibit polynomial complexity in problem size, while specially constructed regression problems can have exponentially complex paths. The authors use smoothed analysis to investigate how those two observations can coexist without dismissing either one.

Their analysis assumes that the observed data contains a tiny amount of intrinsic noise. Under that assumption, they prove polynomial path complexity. The result explains how small perturbations can change the relevant complexity picture, even though exponential constructions exist. It is a statement about the whole path under the analyzed noise setting, rather than a claim that every possible Lasso instance has a short path.
icml-2018-the-well-tempered-lasso-fb640a.tldr: Smoothed analysis shows polynomial Lasso regularization-path complexity under a small intrinsic-noise assumption, helping reconcile empirical behavior with exponential worst cases.

paragraphs: LSTM networks use gates to regulate information flow during sequence processing. In standard implementations, those gates can remain partially open. This paper proposes training that pushes their outputs toward zero or one, making them mostly closed or open and giving their behavior a clearer interpretation.

The change might appear to reduce the model’s flexibility, but the empirical studies report comparable or better performance with no performance drop. The authors attribute this behavior to better generalization. The result supports the possibility that encouraging more decisive gating can improve how a model uses its capacity, rather than requiring intermediate gate values everywhere.

The experiments also find that gate outputs are relatively insensitive to their inputs, enabling several forms of compression. The paper explores low-rank and low-precision approximations, and the compressed models outperform the uncompressed baselines in the reported studies. The findings therefore connect a training change aimed at information flow with both interpretability and empirical robustness to compression; the gates are encouraged toward binary values rather than claimed to be universally exact binary switches.
icml-2018-towards-binary-valued-gates-fo.tldr: Training LSTM gates toward zero or one yields clearer gating and supports compression while maintaining or improving reported performance.

paragraphs: Machine teaching asks how a teacher can guide a learner toward a desired model efficiently. This paper studies a difficult version in which teacher and learner use different feature representations and the teacher cannot fully inspect the learner’s model. That mismatch makes the learner’s current status something the teacher must estimate.

The proposed active teacher queries the learner through exam-like interactions. Responses provide information about the learner’s status, which the teacher then uses to guide subsequent teaching. The authors prove that this process can achieve faster convergence than traditional passive learning and provide sample-complexity results for both teaching and querying.

Experiments compare the active teacher with an omniscient teacher and verify the active model’s effectiveness. The contribution is a way to make progress toward black-box teaching despite differing representations and incomplete visibility. Its mechanism depends on active access to the learner through queries: the teacher can gather evidence about learning progress even when it cannot directly observe the full internal model.
icml-2018-towards-black-box-iterative-ma.tldr: An active teacher uses learner queries to guide faster convergence despite different feature representations and incomplete access to the learner’s model.
